A transcript is a written record of something. That "something" is usually either:

  • Words that were spoken (converted into written form), or
  • Important facts and data about a person or event, captured in an official document.

Think of a transcript as a faithful written copy that preserves something — so it can be read, stored, studied, or referred to later.

1. A Written Record of Spoken Words

When people speak — in a conversation, a court hearing, a podcast, a job interview, a speech, or a meeting — those words disappear into the air the moment they are said. A transcript captures those spoken words and writes them down, so they are permanently preserved.

The goal is usually to be word-for-word accurate. A transcript is not a summary. A summary shortens and simplifies. A transcript tries to record everything that was actually said, as faithfully as possible.

Real-life examples:

  • A court transcript is a written record of everything said during a trial — by the judge, lawyers, witnesses, and everyone else. Every single word is recorded.
  • A podcast or video transcript is the written version of what the speakers said during the episode, so people can read it instead of listening.
  • An interview transcript is the written record of questions and answers from an interview.
  • A speech transcript is the full written text of a speech that was delivered out loud.

A helpful way to think about it: Imagine someone pressed "Record" on a conversation, and then a person carefully listened to that recording and typed out every single word. The document they produced is the transcript.

2. An Official Record of a Person's Academic History

This is a specific and very common use of the word, especially in education. An academic transcript (also called a "school transcript" or "college transcript") is an official document issued by a school, college, or university. It lists:

  • Every course or subject a student studied
  • The grade or score they received in each course
  • The time period they studied

It is essentially the official written history of your academic life at that institution.

This type of transcript is important because it acts as proof. When you apply for a job or to another university, they may ask for your transcript to verify what you studied and how you performed.

A helpful way to think about it: Think of it as your school's official "report card history" — a complete, certified record, not just one term's grades.
The Key Qualities That Define Any Transcript

No matter which type it is, a transcript always has these qualities:

It is a record, not the original. A transcript represents something else — a conversation that happened, or a student's academic journey. It is always a written copy or account of something that exists (or happened) separately.

It aims for completeness and accuracy. A transcript is not supposed to leave things out or change things. Its value comes from being a reliable and thorough record. This is especially true for spoken-word transcripts, where accuracy is critical (for example, in legal proceedings).

It is often official and carries authority. Academic transcripts, for instance, are issued and stamped by the institution itself, making them certified and trustworthy documents. Unofficial transcripts also exist (for example, a copy you download yourself), but they may not be accepted in formal situations where an official, verified copy is required.

Understanding what something is not sharpens the definition:

  • A transcript is not a summary. A summary condenses and leaves things out. A transcript aims to be complete.
  • A transcript is not a paraphrase. A paraphrase rewrites things in different words. A spoken-word transcript records the actual words used.
  • A transcript is not rough notes. Notes are informal and incomplete. A transcript is a deliberate, structured, complete record.

For spoken-word transcripts, there is sometimes a small practical choice made: some transcripts clean up minor speech habits like "um," "uh," or false starts (saying half a word, then correcting yourself), especially when the purpose is readability. Others keep every single sound. The important thing is that neither version changes the meaning of what was said — the substance remains perfectly faithful to the original.

A transcript is a written record that preserves something accurately and completely — either the spoken words of a conversation, hearing, interview, or speech, or the official academic history of a student. Its entire purpose is to serve as a reliable, written representation of something, so it can be referred to, stored, or verified at any time.
